title: GMAT Focus Verbal Practice Test 9
instructions: Original exam-style practice test with answers and explanations.

questions.prompt: An airport opened additional security lanes and reports that the average time passengers spend in the security queue has fallen. Airport management concludes that passengers now arrive at their gates earlier.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the conclusion?
options: A. Passengers who know the queue is shorter now arrive at the airport later than before, and gate arrival times are unchanged.
B. Some passengers have priority access to a separate lane.
C. The new lanes were expensive to install.
D. Security staff report that the work is less stressful.
E. Queue times vary by time of day.
questions.explanation: Travellers reallocate the saved time to arriving later, so the intermediate measure improves without the outcome changing — the same adaptive response that erodes many capacity gains.

questions.prompt: A food authority found that a quarter of honey samples sold in the country contained added syrup, and proposes requiring producers to state the country of origin on the label in order to reduce adulteration.
questions.question: The proposal depends on which of the following assumptions?
options: A. Consumers prefer domestically produced honey.
B. Adding syrup to honey is currently legal.
C. Producers can determine the origin of the honey they sell.
D. Adulteration is concentrated in honey from identifiable origins, so that labelling gives buyers a means of avoiding it.
E. Testing for adulteration is expensive.
questions.explanation: An origin label reduces adulteration only if origin correlates with it; if adulterated and genuine honey come from everywhere alike, the label carries no useful information. D is a feasibility condition but a weaker requirement than the causal one.

questions.prompt: A university library abolished fines for overdue books and reports that the average time books are kept has risen only slightly, while the number of books borrowed has risen sharply. The librarian concludes that fines were deterring borrowing more than they were encouraging prompt return.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the conclusion?
options: A. The library has extended its opening hours.
B. Fine income had been a small part of the library's budget.
C. Surveys before the change found that many students avoided borrowing because they feared incurring fines they could not afford.
D. Some books are now returned later than the previous limit.
E. The library has purchased additional copies of popular titles.
questions.explanation: Direct evidence of the deterrent mechanism, from before the change, supports the causal reading of the rise. A and E introduce rival explanations for increased borrowing.

questions.prompt: A city installed public charging points for electric vehicles in residential streets and reports that electric vehicle ownership in those streets has risen faster than in comparable streets without them. A councillor concludes that installing chargers causes people to buy electric vehicles.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the conclusion?
options: A. Charging points are more expensive to install on narrow streets.
B. The city installed the points in the streets where residents had petitioned for them.
C. Some residents charge their vehicles at work.
D. Electric vehicle prices fell nationally during the period.
E. The chargers are used by residents of neighbouring streets as well.
questions.explanation: Petitioning identifies streets whose residents already intended to buy, so the ownership difference may precede the chargers entirely. D affects both groups and so cannot explain the gap between them.

questions.prompt: Every dental practice in the Warfield area that recalls patients every six months also employs a hygienist. No practice employing a hygienist has been rated below 'good' in the most recent inspection. Some practices in the area were rated below 'good'.
questions.question: If the statements above are true, which of the following must be true?
options: A. Practices employing hygienists provide better treatment.
B. Every practice rated 'good' employs a hygienist.
C. Most practices in the area recall patients every six months.
D. No practice in the area was rated below 'good'.
E. Some practices in the area do not recall patients every six months.
questions.explanation: Practices rated below good exist; such a practice has no hygienist, and six-month recall implies a hygienist, so those practices do not use six-month recall. B asserts causation and E contradicts a premise.

questions.prompt: Since a charge for single-use carrier bags was introduced, the number of such bags issued by supermarkets has fallen by more than 80 per cent. Supporters cite this as evidence that the charge has reduced plastic waste.
questions.question: Which of the following would be most useful to determine in evaluating the supporters' claim?
options: A. How much revenue the charge has raised
B. Whether shoppers support the charge
C. How many supermarkets operate in the country
D. Whether sales of other plastic bags, such as bin liners previously reused from carrier bags, have risen
E. Whether the charge applies to online deliveries
questions.explanation: The claim is about total plastic waste, not bags issued; substitution toward heavier bought bags is the standard way such a measure fails to deliver the headline reduction.

questions.prompt: A football club moved to a larger stadium and its average attendance rose by 8,000. The club's finance director concludes that the move increased the club's revenue from ticket sales by a proportionate amount.
questions.question: The reasoning is most vulnerable to the criticism that it
options: A. assumes attendance figures are accurately recorded
B. overlooks that many of the additional seats were sold at reduced prices to fill the ground
C. ignores the cost of building the stadium
D. fails to account for away supporters
E. does not consider the club's performance on the field
questions.explanation: Revenue is attendance multiplied by price, and filling a larger ground commonly requires discounting; a proportionate revenue increase does not follow. C is about profit rather than the revenue claim.

questions.prompt: A hotel group found that guests enrolled in its loyalty scheme stay more nights per year than guests who are not, and plans to enrol all guests automatically at check-in in order to increase nights stayed.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, casts most doubt on the plan?
options: A. Guests who travel frequently join loyalty schemes precisely because they expect to stay often.
B. Loyalty schemes are common in the industry.
C. Enrolment requires an email address.
D. Some enrolled guests never claim their rewards.
E. The scheme costs the group little to administer.
questions.explanation: Frequent travellers select into the scheme, so membership marks the behaviour rather than producing it, and automatic enrolment of infrequent guests will not make them frequent.

questions.prompt: An insurer offering crop insurance found that farmers who buy it plant riskier, higher-yielding varieties than farmers who do not. The insurer concludes that offering insurance changes what farmers plant.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the insurer's conclusion?
options: A. Insured farmers own more land on average.
B. Riskier varieties command higher prices in good years.
C. In a district where insurance was offered by lottery, farmers who received it shifted to riskier varieties within two seasons, while those who did not made no such change.
D. The insurer's premiums vary by district.
E. Some uninsured farmers plant riskier varieties.
questions.explanation: A lottery removes the possibility that risk-tolerant farmers simply buy more insurance, which is the alternative reading of the original correlation.

questions.prompt: A tutoring application reports that pupils who complete more than twenty sessions improve their test scores by an average of nine points, and advertises that using the application raises scores by nine points.
questions.question: The advertisement is misleading primarily because
options: A. nine points is a small improvement
B. test scores are not the only measure of learning
C. the application is not free
D. some pupils use other tutoring as well
E. the figure describes only pupils who completed twenty sessions, who may differ systematically from those who did not
questions.explanation: Persistence to twenty sessions is itself a marker of motivation and support; the average across all users would be lower. E is a genuine confound but a smaller one than the completion filter.

questions.prompt: A city council argues that planting street trees will reduce summer temperatures in its centre. A critic replies that the council has failed to fund maintenance for trees already planted, a third of which have died.
questions.question: The critic's reply is best understood as
options: A. denying that trees reduce temperatures
B. arguing that the trees chosen are unsuitable for urban conditions
C. claiming that the council has misrepresented the temperature data
D. questioning whether the proposed benefit will materialise given the council's record of implementation
E. proposing an alternative method of cooling the city centre
questions.explanation: The reply grants the mechanism and attacks delivery, which is the strongest form of the objection available on the facts given.

questions.passageTitle: The Rise and Fall of the Conglomerate
questions.passageText:
For roughly two decades after 1960, large firms in several countries assembled portfolios of unrelated businesses. The rationale offered was diversification: earnings from businesses whose fortunes moved independently would be steadier than earnings from any one of them, and a firm with internal capital could move funds to whichever division had the best opportunities.

The first half of that argument was always weak. A shareholder can diversify by holding shares in several firms, at negligible cost, and does not need a conglomerate to do it. Diversification within the firm is valuable to managers, whose careers are undiversified, more than to the owners on whose behalf it is nominally undertaken.

The second half is more serious and was rarely tested. An internal capital market can beat an external one where outsiders cannot assess a division's prospects, which is plausible for research-intensive or specialised businesses. Whether headquarters actually allocates well is an empirical matter, and studies of internal allocation have often found funds flowing toward divisions with political weight rather than good prospects.

By the 1980s conglomerates commonly traded below the estimated value of their divisions sold separately. The discount is not fully explained: it may reflect poor allocation, the difficulty of valuing an opaque group, or entrenchment that resists breaking the firm up. What is clear is that the wave of divestment which followed was not simply a fashion in the opposite direction. It reversed a structure whose stated justification had a redundant half and an unverified half, and the burden of evidence had never been discharged.
questions.prompt: The author regards the diversification rationale for conglomerates as
options: A. redundant, since shareholders can diversify for themselves at low cost
B. sound in principle but poorly executed
C. applicable only to firms in cyclical industries
D. the strongest of the arguments offered
E. impossible to evaluate without internal data
questions.explanation: The second paragraph calls the first half of the argument weak for exactly this reason, and adds that diversification serves managers, whose careers are undiversified.

questions.passageText:
Every animal studied closely enough shows a state resembling sleep, and the cost of that state is considerable: an animal asleep is not feeding, not mating, and less able to detect a predator. A behaviour so costly and so universal is generally taken to indicate a function of comparable importance. Identifying it has proved unexpectedly hard.

The most durable proposals fall into three groups. The first is restorative: sleep permits repair and clearance of metabolic products that accumulate during waking, a proposal strengthened by evidence that clearance of certain substances from brain tissue increases during sleep. The second concerns memory: patterns of neural activity from waking are replayed during sleep, and disrupting particular sleep stages impairs retention of material learned beforehand. The third is regulatory, treating sleep as a mechanism for enforcing inactivity when activity would be unproductive or dangerous, which fits the wide variation in sleep duration across species better than the others.

These are frequently presented as competitors. They need not be. A state that occupies a third of an animal's life and involves the whole brain is unlikely to serve one function only, and the assumption that a single answer must be correct has probably slowed the field.

What can be said with confidence is narrower than popular accounts suggest. Sleep is homeostatically regulated, its loss produces measurable deficits, and no organism has been shown to forgo it entirely. Why exactly it is required remains, after a century of investigation, an open question with several partial answers.
questions.prompt: The passage indicates that sleep is generally assumed to serve an important function because
options: A. it occupies a third of an animal's life
B. it can be disrupted experimentally
C. it is costly and universal among animals studied closely
D. it involves the whole brain
E. its absence is invariably fatal
questions.explanation: The inference from cost plus universality is stated in the first paragraph. E overstates: the passage says no organism has been shown to forgo sleep, not that its absence is always fatal.

questions.passageText:
Poverty can be measured against a fixed basket of goods or against the distribution of income in the society being examined. The choice is not technical, and confusing the two produces arguments in which neither side is quite wrong.

An absolute measure fixes a threshold — the income needed to purchase specified food, shelter and other necessities — and adjusts it only for prices. It has the advantage of registering real improvement: if incomes at the bottom rise, absolute poverty falls, whatever happens elsewhere in the distribution. Its weakness is that the basket dates. A definition of necessity drawn up when few households had refrigeration or telephones does not describe what is required to participate in a society where employers, schools and public services assume both.

A relative measure sets the threshold at a proportion of median income. It captures the sense in which poverty is exclusion from the ordinary life of a society rather than a level of consumption, and it updates automatically. Its notorious weakness is that it can move for reasons that have nothing to do with the poor: a fall in median income during a recession reduces measured relative poverty without anyone at the bottom being better off.

Statistical agencies increasingly publish both, along with measures anchored to a past year's relative threshold. The reason is not indecision. The two measures answer different questions — one about deprivation, one about inequality of participation — and a country can improve on either while worsening on the other.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, an advantage of an absolute measure of poverty is that it
options: A. adjusts automatically as a society becomes richer
B. is unaffected by changes in prices
C. measures exclusion from ordinary social life
D. registers real improvement when incomes at the bottom rise
E. is easier to compute than a relative measure
questions.explanation: Absolute measures record improvement at the bottom regardless of what happens elsewhere. C is false: such measures are adjusted for prices.

options: A. They cannot be compared across countries.
B. They ignore the cost of housing.
C. They require annual household surveys.

questions.passageText:
The replacement of the scroll by the codex — leaves stacked and bound along one edge, the form we still call a book — took place over several centuries in the Roman world, and the reasons for it illuminate how a format shapes what can be done with a text.

Practical advantages were real. A codex holds more text than a scroll of comparable bulk, since both sides of each leaf can be written on; it is more robust; and it is cheaper for a given quantity of text. But these advantages were available long before the transition completed, which suggests they were not decisive on their own.

The more interesting advantage is random access. Consulting a passage in a scroll requires unrolling to the place; a codex can be opened at a point and compared with another. This matters little for a work read continuously from beginning to end, and a great deal for a text used for reference, comparison and citation — and the early adoption of the codex by Christian communities, whose practice involved cross-referencing scriptural texts, fits that pattern, whatever additional reasons of group identity may also have applied.

The episode suggests a general point. The advantages of a format are not fixed properties but depend on what readers do with texts, and a change in reading practice can make a long-available technology suddenly decisive. Similar arguments have been made about the index, the page number and the search box, none of which changed what a text contained and all of which changed what could be done with one.
questions.prompt: The passage suggests that the practical advantages of the codex were not decisive on their own because
options: A. they were disputed by contemporary writers
B. they were available long before the transition was complete
C. scrolls were cheaper to produce
D. few readers could afford either format
E. the advantages applied only to short texts
questions.explanation: The second paragraph makes exactly this argument from timing.

A relative measure sets the threshold at a proportion of median income. It captures the sense in which poverty is exclusion from the ordinary life of a society rather than a level of consumption, and it updates automatically. Its notorious weakness is that it can move for reasons that have nothing to do with the poor: a fall in median income during a recession reduces measured relative poverty without anyone at the bottom being better off.

Statistical agencies increasingly publish both, along with measures anchored to a past year's relative threshold. The reason is not indecision. The two measures answer different questions — one about deprivation, one about inequality of participation — and a country can improve on either while worsening on the other.

readingPassages.title: From Scroll to Codex
readingPassages.text:
The replacement of the scroll by the codex — leaves stacked and bound along one edge, the form we still call a book — took place over several centuries in the Roman world, and the reasons for it illuminate how a format shapes what can be done with a text.

Practical advantages were real. A codex holds more text than a scroll of comparable bulk, since both sides of each leaf can be written on; it is more robust; and it is cheaper for a given quantity of text. But these advantages were available long before the transition completed, which suggests they were not decisive on their own.

The more interesting advantage is random access. Consulting a passage in a scroll requires unrolling to the place; a codex can be opened at a point and compared with another. This matters little for a work read continuously from beginning to end, and a great deal for a text used for reference, comparison and citation — and the early adoption of the codex by Christian communities, whose practice involved cross-referencing scriptural texts, fits that pattern, whatever additional reasons of group identity may also have applied.

The episode suggests a general point. The advantages of a format are not fixed properties but depend on what readers do with texts, and a change in reading practice can make a long-available technology suddenly decisive. Similar arguments have been made about the index, the page number and the search box, none of which changed what a text contained and all of which changed what could be done with one.
